questions.intro: Some actions are CONSEQUENTIAL: hard or impossible to undo, or affecting other people. Examples: SENDING messages, making PAYMENTS, DELETING data, and PUBLISHING content. A safe automation pauses before these and asks a person to APPROVE, showing exactly what will happen ("Send this email to 120 parents?" with the text). This is called HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP review. Low-stakes, reversible steps, such as drafting or sorting, can run without approval. The person approving should actually read the details, not click "yes" by habit.

sections.skill: Compare approval with a parent signing a permission slip

questions.prompt: When must the parent sign?
questions.intro: A school does not take students on a trip just because a teacher planned it. A PARENT reads the permission slip (where, when, cost) and SIGNS before the trip happens. A signature after the trip would be pointless. Small things, like what game to play at recess, need no slip. Human approval in automation works the same way: a person reads the details and approves BEFORE consequential actions, while small steps go ahead.

sections.skill: Avoid approval fatigue and split actions

questions.prompt: What is approval fatigue?

choices.text: Feeling tired after approving one very important request that took a long time to read
Clicking yes by habit because there are too many requests

questions.correct_answer: Clicking yes by habit because there are too many requests
questions.intro: Approval can fail quietly. If every small step asks for approval, people stop reading and click yes automatically, called APPROVAL FATIGUE. Ask only for consequential steps, and show clear details: who, what, how much. Watch for actions split into many small ones that each look harmless, such as 50 separate one-dollar payments. And approval must happen BEFORE the action; reviewing a log afterward cannot unsend an email.
